IS_C01_INTRO1::block-0:
The mantras beginning with 'īśā vāsyam' have not been employed in (any sacrificial) rites; for they reveal the true nature of the Self, which is not an accessory to action. The true nature of the Self — its purity, its untouchedness by sin (apāpaviddhatva), its oneness, eternality, bodilessness, all-pervadingness, and so forth — will be set forth (in this very Upaniṣad). And such a nature stands opposed to action; hence the non-employment of these mantras in rites is altogether fitting. For the true nature of the Self, marked by such characteristics, is not something to be brought into being, modified, attained, or refined, nor is it of the form of an agent or experiencer — by which it might become subordinate to action. Indeed, all the Upaniṣads exhaust themselves in nothing but the determination of the true nature of the Self; and the Bhagavad-gītā and the Mokṣa-dharma sections likewise have this very purport.

Therefore, presupposing the Self's apparent multiplicity, agency, experience-hood, and the like, and likewise its (apparent) impurity and contamination by sin — all of which are established only by ordinary worldly cognition — rites have been enjoined. For he who is desirous of the fruit of action, whether seen (such as Brahmanical lustre and so on) or unseen (such as heaven and the rest), and who regards himself thus — 'I am twice-born, I am furnished with no disqualifying defect such as one-eyedness, hunchbackedness, and the like' — he alone is qualified for rites. So declare those who know the rules of qualification (adhikāra).

Therefore these mantras, by revealing the true nature of the Self, dispel that natural (and false) cognition concerning the Self which assumes it to be an agent of action, and thereby produce the knowledge of the Self's oneness — which is the means of severing sorrow, delusion, and the other attributes of saṃsāra. Thus, having stated the qualified hearer (adhikārin), the subject-matter (abhidheya), the relation (sambandha), and the purpose (prayojana), we shall now expound the mantras concisely —
IS_C01_V01: By the Lord must all this be enveloped — whatsoever moves in this moving world. By that renunciation enjoy thou; covet not anyone's wealth.
IS_C01_V01::block-0:
'Īśā' — 'īṣṭe' (he rules), so 'īṭ', and by Him, 'īśā'. The Ruler is the supreme Lord, the supreme Self of all. For He alone rules over all, being the Self of all beings, in the form of the inmost Self (pratyagātman). By Him — that is, by one's own true form, by the Self — is this all to be enveloped (vāsyam, lit. 'covered as with a garment'). Enveloped with what? — With this: 'Whatsoever moves on the earth (jagatī), all of that.'

By one's own Self, who is the Lord, in the form of the inmost Self — by the perception of the supremely real form, 'I alone am all this' — must this entire unreal moving and unmoving world be covered over with one's own supreme Self. Just as the foul smell arising adventitiously in sandalwood, aloe-wood and the like, born of contact with water and so forth, is covered over by rubbing forth its (own) form — by its own true and natural fragrance — even so the duality of the world, with its characteristic of agency and experience-hood, superimposed (adhyasta) upon one's own Self as if natural to it, on the earth — and 'on the earth' here is by way of indication, hence the entire host of modifications called name, form, and action — all this is to be relinquished by the contemplation of the supremely real Self.

Thus, for one yoked to the contemplation of the Lord-as-Self, qualification lies only in the renunciation of the three cravings — for sons, wealth, and worlds — and not in rites. 'By that renunciation' (tena tyaktena) — the meaning is 'by renunciation itself.' For a relinquished, that is, a dead, son or servant does not protect oneself, since he no longer stands in any relation to oneself; therefore the meaning is precisely 'by renunciation.' 'Bhuñjīthāḥ' — protect (or cherish) thyself. Being thus one whose cravings are relinquished, 'mā gṛdhaḥ' — make not (any) gṛdhi, longing, with regard to wealth. 'Whose wealth?' (kasya svid dhanam) — covet not the wealth of any other or of thy own self; this is the meaning. 'Svit' is a particle without independent meaning.

Or else: 'covet not!' Why? — 'Whose wealth (could there be)?' — taken as a rhetorical refutation: there is no wealth belonging to anyone that one might covet. By the contemplation 'I am the Lord; this all is the Self alone,' the all has been renounced. Hence this all belongs to the Self alone, and the Self alone is all. Therefore covet not, for its object is unreal — this is the meaning.
IS_C01_V02: Performing rites here itself, may one wish to live a hundred years. Thus — and not otherwise than this — does action not cling to thee, the man.
IS_C01_V02::block-0: Thus, by the renunciation of the three cravings — for sons and the rest — and by establishment in the knowledge of the Self (ātmajñāna-niṣṭhā), the Self of the knower of the Self is to be safeguarded: this is the meaning of the (preceding) Vedic passage. Now, for the other — for him who, being ignorant of the Self, is incapable of grasping the Self — this (next) mantra teaches —
IS_C01_V02::block-1:
'Performing them indeed,' i.e. accomplishing them, here itself — that is, the Agnihotra and the rest — let one wish to live (jijīviṣet) a hundred years (samāḥ — saṃvatsarān, samāḥ being years numbering one hundred). For that has been laid down as the maximum lifespan of a human being. And accordingly, by way of restating what is (anyway) attained, what is enjoined is precisely this: 'should one wish to live a hundred years, one should do so only while performing rites.'

'Evam' — in this way; 'tvayi' — in thee, who, identifying thyself merely as a man (naramātra-abhimānī), wishest to live; 'itaḥ' — than this present mode, namely, the performance of rites such as the Agnihotra; there is no other mode (anyathā nāsti) by which inauspicious karma may not cling. The meaning is: thou shalt not be tainted by action. Hence, while performing the rites enjoined by the śāstra — Agnihotra and the rest — let one wish to live.
IS_C01_V02::block-2:
Objection: But how is it understood that by the previous mantra (jñāna-niṣṭhā), the establishment in knowledge, has been declared for the renouncer (saṃnyāsin), while by this second one, establishment in action (karma-niṣṭhā) has been declared for him who is incapable of that?

Reply: Dost thou not remember the contradiction between knowledge and action — unshakeable as a mountain — that has already been stated? Here too it has been said: 'He who would wish to live, let him do so only while performing rites'; and also (in the previous mantra): 'By the Lord must all this be enveloped,' 'Enjoy by that renunciation, covet not anyone's wealth.' And by the injunction concerning saṃnyāsa: 'Let him not entertain craving either for life or death; let him repair to the forest — that is the (final) station; let him not return from there.' Furthermore, the Upaniṣad will declare the difference of fruit between the two. 'These two indeed are the paths that have come down distinct: the path of action in the foremost place, and saṃnyāsa' — the latter being the path of nivṛtti, the renunciation of the three cravings. Of these two, saṃnyāsa is preferred above (atyaricat) — 'nyāsa eva atyarecat' (Tai. Nārā. 78), so says the Taittirīya. 'These two paths, indeed, are those wherein the Vedas are established: dharma marked by pravṛtti, and that distinguished as nivṛtti' (Mokṣa-dharma 241.6) — and so on. This was, after due deliberation, definitively pronounced by Vyāsa, the venerable teacher of the Vedas, to his son. The division between these two we shall display (further on).
IS_C01_V03: Demonic-realm (asurya), indeed, are those worlds, enveloped by blinding darkness. To them, after death, do those people repair — whosoever they be that are slayers of the Self.
IS_C01_V03::block-0: Now, at this point, this mantra is begun, the purport of which is to censure the unenlightened —
IS_C01_V03::block-1:
'Asuryāḥ' — having regard to the supreme Self-state, which is non-dual, even the gods and the rest are 'asuras' (i.e., not on a par with that). The worlds that pertain to them are accordingly called 'asurya' by name. The word 'nāma' is a particle without independent meaning. 'Loka' — those worlds are the fruits of action; for the meaning is that births are 'lokyante,' i.e. seen, experienced. They are 'enveloped, covered over, by blinding darkness' — that is, by ignorance, whose very nature is non-perception.

To them — to the (worlds of) beings down to the immobile (sthāvara) — they 'pretya,' having departed from this body, 'abhigacchanti,' resort, each according to his action and according to what he has heard. 'Whosoever' — 'ye ke ca' — 'ātmahanaḥ,' slayers of the Self, since they slay the Self. Who? 'Te janāḥ' — those people who are unenlightened.

Objection: But how do they slay the eternal Self?

Reply: By veiling, through the defect of avidyā, the Self that ever exists. The fruit of the existing Self — namely, the experiencing of unageingness, immortality, and the like — becomes, as it were, hidden, just as in one slain. Hence the ordinary, unenlightened folk are termed 'slayers of the Self.' For it is by that very defect of self-slaying that they undergo saṃsāra.
IS_C01_V04: Unmoving, one, swifter than mind — the gods do not attain it; it has gone before them as they ran. Standing still, it overtakes others that run; therein Mātariśvan apportions the activities.
IS_C01_V04::block-0: By the slaying of which Self the unenlightened transmigrate, and conversely by being non-slayers of which Self the wise are liberated — what is the nature of that Self? This is now told —
IS_C01_V04::block-1:
'Anejat' — not 'ejat'; 'eju kampane' (the root 'ej' in the sense of trembling); 'kampana' is motion, falling away from one's own state. 'Anejat,' therefore, means devoid of that — ever of one form, is the meaning. And that is one (ekam) in all beings. 'Manaso javīyaḥ' — swifter than the mind, whose mark is volition and the rest.

Objection: How can two contradictories be asserted — that this is firm, motionless, and (also) swifter than the mind?

Reply: This is no fault, for it is feasible (when one views the Self) as without and as with limiting adjuncts (upādhi). Of these two, by its own form free of upādhis it is described as 'unmoving and one'; but on account of its following the upādhi of the inner organ — the mind, marked by volition and doubt — (it is described as 'swifter'). Here, of the mind situated in the body, the volition concerning a thing far away, like Brahmaloka, takes place in but a moment; hence the swiftness of the mind is well known in the world.

When this mind, swiftly going to Brahmaloka and the rest, is moving, the reflection of the consciousness of the Self (ātma-caitanyābhāsa) appears, as it were, attained first (before all else). Hence it is said: 'swifter than the mind.' 'The gods' — the dyotanāt (from 'shining'), the senses such as the eye and the rest — 'na enad āpnuvan,' did not attain this Self-principle here under discussion. The mind is swifter than they; and since the operation of the senses is mediated by the operation of the mind, even a mere semblance of the Self never falls within the scope of these gods. Because, by reason of (its) swiftness, it has gone before even the mind (pūrvam arṣat), being all-pervasive like space.

The all-pervading Self-principle, divested of all attributes of saṃsāra, by its own form free of upādhi, ever undergoing no transformation — yet in the eyes of the undiscerning and deluded, it appears, as it were, to undergo all the modifications of saṃsāra brought about by the upādhis, and seems many, as it were, in each body. This is what is now said: 'tat dhāvataḥ' — running swiftly; 'anyān' — others, namely, the mind, speech, the senses, and so on, which are different in kind from the Self; 'atyeti' — overtakes, as it were, surpassing them. The 'as it were' (iva) sense He himself shows by 'tiṣṭhat' — that is, while remaining itself unmodified.

'Tasmin' — when this Self-principle exists, of the nature of eternal consciousness; 'mātariśvā' — he who 'śvayati' (moves, blows) in the 'mātṛ' (the mid-region), is Mātariśvan, the wind, of the form of the activity sustaining all life-breaths, on which depend the aggregates of the bodily effects (kārya) and instruments (karaṇa), and in which all are warped and woofed; that which, designated by the term sūtra, is the upholder of the entire universe — that is Mātariśvan. 'Apaḥ' — the activities, characterised by the movement of all living beings, and characterised by the burning, consuming, illumining, and raining of fire, sun, cloud, and so on. 'Dadhāti' — apportions, that is, distributes; or, sustains. So is established by śrutis such as 'Through fear of him the wind blows,' and so forth. The meaning is: every modification of effect and instrument takes place only when the Self of the nature of eternal consciousness, which is the substratum of all, exists.
IS_C01_V05: It moves, and it moves not. It is far, and it is near. It is within all this, and it is also without all this.
IS_C01_V05::block-0: Since there is no redundancy among the mantras (na mantrāṇāṃ jāmitā asti), the meaning already stated in the previous mantra is repeated again —
IS_C01_V05::block-1:
'Tat' — that Self-principle here under discussion — 'ejati,' moves; and the very same 'na ejati,' does not move from itself. 'Of itself it is unmoving, but appears as if moving' — that is the sense. Furthermore, 'tat dūre' — far away, since for the unenlightened it is unattainable even by hundreds of crores of years, hence as if far. 'Tat u antike' — and yet near, exceedingly so for the wise, for it is the very Self; not merely far, but also near.

'Tat antaḥ' — within, of all this, in accordance with the śruti 'He who is the Self, the inmost of all,' that is, of all this universe whose nature is name, form, and action. 'Tat tu sarvasya asya bāhyataḥ' — but the same is also without all this; on account of all-pervadingness, it is within like space (ākāśa); and on account of unsurpassed subtlety; and 'continuously,' from the teaching 'a mass of pure consciousness alone' (Bṛ. 4.5.13), there is no interstice.
IS_C01_V06: But he who beholds all beings in the Self alone, and the Self in all beings — thence does he not turn away in disgust.
IS_C01_V06::block-0:
'Yastu' — but he who, being a parivrāṭ, a seeker of liberation (mumukṣu), 'sarvāṇi bhūtāni,' all beings from the unmanifest down to the immobile, 'ātmany eva anupaśyati,' beholds in the Self alone — beholds nothing as distinct from the Self, that is the meaning. And 'sarva-bhūteṣu ca ātmānam' — and the Self in those very beings — beholds the Self of those beings as their very Self.

Just as the Self of this body, which is the aggregate of effects and instruments, is myself — the witness of all cognitions, the conscious one, alone, attributeless — even with this very form, 'I myself am the Self of all beings from the unmanifest down to the immobile' — thus does he behold the Self in all beings as devoid of distinction.

'Saḥ' — he, 'tataḥ,' from that very vision, 'na vijugupsate,' does not give rise to vijugupsā (revulsion), to disgust. This is but a restatement of what is already attained. For all disgust arises in one who sees something tainted as other than the Self; for one who sees only the Self — utterly pure, continuous — there exists no other thing to occasion disgust. Hence it is already attained — that 'thence he does not turn away in disgust.'
IS_C01_V07: When all beings have become one's very Self for the man of right vision, what delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who beholds the oneness?
IS_C01_V07::block-0: Another mantra also expresses this very same purport —
IS_C01_V07::block-1:
'Yasmin sarvāṇi bhūtāni' — at the time, or in the Self as expounded, in which all those very beings 'ātmaiva abhūt' — became the Self alone, were resolved into the Self alone, by the vision of the supremely real Self, 'vijānataḥ' — for the knower of the supremely real entity; 'tatra' — at that time, or in that Self; 'ko mohaḥ kaḥ śokaḥ' — what delusion, what sorrow?

Sorrow and delusion arise in him who has not known the seed (bīja) of desire and action; not, however, in him who beholds the oneness of the Self — pure, like unto the sky. By the rhetorical 'what delusion, what sorrow?' — through the implication of impossibility (asambhava-prakāśanāt) of sorrow and delusion, which are effects of avidyā — the utter, absolute uprooting of saṃsāra, together with its cause, is shown.
IS_C01_V08: He pervaded all — bright, bodiless, woundless, sinewless, pure, untouched by sin; the seer, the thinker, all-encompassing, self-existent — He apportioned objects, each according to its true nature, for the everlasting years.
IS_C01_V08::block-0: The Self that has been spoken of in the preceding mantras — when standing forth in His own true form, of what description is He? This mantra answers —
IS_C01_V08::block-1:
*Sa paryagāt* — that Self of whom we have spoken *paryagāt*: *pari* (all around) + *agāt* (went, pervaded) — that is, He pervades like ākāśa. *Śukram* — bright, luminous, possessed of effulgence; resplendent is the meaning. *Akāyam* — without body, devoid of the subtle (liṅga) body. *Avraṇam* — unwounded, without injury. *Asnāviram* — *snāvas* are the sinews; that in which sinews do not exist is *asnāviram*. By these two — *avraṇam* and *asnāviram* — the gross body is denied of Him. *Śuddham* — pure, stainless, free from the taint of avidyā: by this the causal body is denied. *Apāpaviddham* — untouched by sin in the form of dharma, adharma and the rest.

The words beginning with *śukram* must be construed in the masculine, since the passage opens with *sa paryagāt* (masculine) and concludes again with *kavir manīṣī* and the rest in the masculine. *Kavi* — the seer beyond, the all-seeing one, in accord with the śruti, *nānyo'to'sti draṣṭā* (Bṛ. Up. 3.7.23), "there is no other seer than This." *Manīṣī* — the ruler of the mind (*manasa īṣitā*); the omniscient Lord (Īśvara) is what is meant. *Paribhūḥ* — He who exists above (*pari upari bhavati*) all; hence *paribhūḥ*. *Svayambhūḥ* — He who exists of Himself; both those above whom He stands and He Himself who stands above all — He alone exists of Himself; therefore *svayambhū*.

That eternally liberated Lord, by reason of His omniscience — *yāthātathyataḥ*: the state of being just-as-it-truly-is is *yāthātathya*; thence, in accordance with the means yielding the fruits of works exactly as they are — *arthān*, the objects to be performed (the duties), *vyadadhāt*, He apportioned, that is, distributed each according to fitness. *Śāśvatībhyaḥ samābhyaḥ* — to the eternal years, that is, to the Prajāpatis named the year-cycles.
IS_C01_V09: Into blinding darkness enter those who worship avidyā; into still greater darkness, as it were, those who delight in vidyā alone.
IS_C01_V09::block-0:
Here, in the opening mantra — *īśāvāsyam idaṁ sarvam … mā gṛdhaḥ kasya svid dhanam* (Īśā Up. 1) — the first sense of the Veda has been declared: jñāna-niṣṭhā by way of renunciation of all longings. Then, since jñāna-niṣṭhā is impossible for the unenlightened who wish to live, the second sense of the Veda has been declared in *kurvann eveha karmāṇi jijīviṣet* (Īśā Up. 2): karma-niṣṭhā.

The distinction between these two niṣṭhās — pointed out by the two mantras — is also shown in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka. By *so'kāmayata jāyā me syāt* (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.17) and the rest, works are prescribed for the ignorant man who has desires; and from *mana evāsyātmā vāg jāyā* (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.17; 1.5.2), one ascertains with certainty that the karma-niṣṭha is both ignorant and afflicted with desire. Accordingly, his fruit is the creation of the seven kinds of food, and abiding in those as identical with one's own self.

Furthermore, for the knowers of Ātman, by renunciation of the threefold longing — for wife, wealth, and worlds — niṣṭhā in the Self's own form alone, hostile to karma-niṣṭhā, has been shown: *kiṁ prajayā kariṣyāmo yeṣāṁ no'yam ātmāyaṁ lokaḥ* (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.22), and so on.

Now, for those jñāna-niṣṭhā saṁnyāsins, beginning with *asuryā nāma te* (Īśā Up. 3) — by way of censuring the unenlightened — the true nature of the Self has been taught up to *sa paryagāt* (Īśā Up. 8). They alone are qualified here, not the desire-bound. So too in the Mantropaniṣad of the Śvetāśvataras, with the same division: *atyāśramibhyaḥ paramaṁ pavitraṁ provāca samyag ṛṣi-saṅgha-juṣṭam* (Śvet. Up. 6.21).

But as for those karma-niṣṭhas, the desirers, who, performing rites alone, wish to live — to them is now addressed *andhaṁ tamaḥ* and the rest.

How is it understood thus, and not for all alike? It is answered: in the case of those without desire, by the cancellation of the very distinction between sādhya (end) and sādhana (means), the realization of the Self's oneness — *yasmin sarvāṇi bhūtāny ātmaivābhūd vijānataḥ. tatra ko mohaḥ kaḥ śoka ekatvam anupaśyataḥ* (Īśā Up. 7) — that knowledge no undeluded man would seek to combine with any rite or any other knowledge. Here, on the contrary, with intent to combine, censure of the unenlightened and so forth is undertaken. And here, what may, by reasoning or by śāstra, be combined with what — that alone is now spoken of.

This daiva-vitta — knowledge whose object is the deities — is set forth as connected with karma; it is not knowledge of the Supreme Self, since a separate fruit is heard of: *vidyayā devalokaḥ* (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.16). Of these two — vidyā (deity-knowledge) and karma — the censure here of practising each one singly is uttered with the intent to combine them, and not as final censure of either, since separate fruits are heard of: *vidyayā tad ārohanti*, *vidyayā devalokaḥ*; *na tatra dakṣiṇā yānti*, *karmaṇā pitṛlokaḥ* (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.16). For nothing enjoined by śāstra can become not-to-be-done. There —
IS_C01_V09::block-1:
*Andhaṁ tamaḥ* — darkness consisting of non-perception, blinding darkness — *praviśanti*, they enter. Who? — *ye avidyām*: "avidyā" here means that which is other than vidyā, namely karma; for karma is opposed to vidyā. That avidyā, of the form of agnihotra and the rest, alone, *upāsate* — they worship; that is, taking it as their highest purpose, they perform it. This is the import.

*Tataḥ* — than that blinding darkness — *bhūya iva*, into still greater darkness, as it were, do they enter. Who? Those who, leaving karma aside, *vidyāyām eva* — in vidyā alone, that is, in the knowledge of the deities alone — *ratāḥ*, are devoted, take supreme delight.
IS_C01_V10: Other indeed, they say, is what is attained by vidyā; other, they say, is what is attained by avidyā. Thus have we heard from the wise who declared it to us.
IS_C01_V10::block-0: Now the difference of intermediate fruit between vidyā and karma is stated as the ground for their combination; for otherwise, when one bears fruit and the other does not, the placing of them side by side as principal and subordinate would amount to mere redundancy (jāmitā) —
IS_C01_V10::block-1: *Anyat* — separate, distinct — *vidyayā kriyate phalam iti āhuḥ*: "the fruit produced by vidyā is one thing," they declare, on the strength of the śruti *vidyayā devalokaḥ*, *vidyayā tad ārohanti*. *Anyad āhur avidyayā*: "another is the fruit produced by avidyā, by karma" — as has been said, *karmaṇā pitṛlokaḥ, vidyayā devalokaḥ* (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.16). *Iti* — thus — *śuśruma*, we have heard, the saying of *dhīrāṇām*, the wise. Those teachers — *ye naḥ tad vicacakṣire* — who explained that, both karma and jñāna, to us; this tradition has come down through the lineage of teachers — that is the meaning.
IS_C01_V11: He who knows both these — vidyā and avidyā — together, crosses death by avidyā and attains immortality by vidyā.
IS_C01_V11::block-1:
*Vidyāṁ ca avidyāṁ ca* — deity-knowledge and karma respectively. He who knows both of these *saha* — together, that is, as to be performed by one and the same person — to him alone, the practitioner of combination, accrues the relation to one human end (puruṣārtha) in due sequence, as is now stated.

*Avidyayā* — by karma, agnihotra and the rest — *mṛtyum*: natural karma along with deity-knowledge is signified by the word *mṛtyu*; that pair he transcends, having crossed it, *vidyayā* — by deity-knowledge — *amṛtam* — the state of becoming one with the deity — *aśnute*, attains. For that *amṛta* is so called — namely, the going to the deity-Self.
IS_C01_V12: Into blinding darkness enter those who worship asambhūti (the unmanifest); into still greater darkness, as it were, those who delight in sambhūti (the manifest).
IS_C01_V12::block-0: Now, with intent to combine the upāsanās of the manifest (vyākṛta) and the unmanifest (avyākṛta), censure of each one severally is uttered —
IS_C01_V12::block-1:
*Andhaṁ tamaḥ praviśanti ye asambhūtim*: *sambhavanam* is *sambhūti* — the coming-to-be of an effect; that of which this *sambhūti* belongs is the effect; *anyā* (other) than that is *asambhūti* — the cause, prakṛti, called avyākṛta. That *asambhūti* — prakṛti, named avyākṛta, the cause, avidyā which is the seed of desire and karma, of the form of non-perception — they who *upāsate*, worship, themselves enter just *andhaṁ tamaḥ* — darkness of the form of non-perception — proportionate to that very upāsanā.

*Tataḥ* — than that itself — *bhūyaḥ* — into still greater darkness, as it were — *te praviśanti ye u* — those who, on the contrary — *sambhūtyāṁ* — in the effect-Brahman, named Hiraṇyagarbha — *ratāḥ*, are devoted.
IS_C01_V13: Other indeed, they say, is what comes from sambhava (the manifest); other, they say, is what comes from asambhava (the unmanifest). Thus have we heard from the wise who declared it to us.
IS_C01_V13::block-0: Now the cause of the combination of the two upāsanās — namely, the difference of the partial fruit — is stated —
IS_C01_V13::block-1: *Anyad eva* — distinct indeed — *āhuḥ phalaṁ sambhavāt*: from sambhūti, that is, from the upāsanā of the effect-Brahman, they have declared the fruit characterized by the powers of aṇimā and the rest — that is the meaning. Likewise, *anyad āhur asambhavāt*: from asambhūti, that is, from the upāsanā of the unmanifest, that fruit which has been spoken of in *andhaṁ tamaḥ praviśanti* (Īśā Up. 9), and which is called by the Pauraṇikas *prakṛti-laya* — dissolution into prakṛti. *Iti* — thus — *śuśruma*, we have heard the saying of the wise. Those — *ye naḥ tad vicacakṣire* — who expounded to us the fruit of the upāsanās of the manifest and the unmanifest.
IS_C01_V14: He who knows both these — sambhūti and vināśa (taken as asambhūti) — together, crosses death by vināśa and attains immortality by sambhūti.
IS_C01_V14::block-0: Since it is so, the combination of the upāsanās of sambhūti and asambhūti is fitting, and that because they are connected with one human end —
IS_C01_V14::block-1:
*Sambhūtiṁ ca vināśaṁ ca yas tad vedobhayaṁ saha*. *Vināśena*: *vināśa* is the attribute (dharma); that effect of which *vināśa* is the attribute is named, by non-difference between dharma and dharmin, simply *vināśa*. By the upāsanā of that — by Hiraṇyagarbha-upāsanā — there is attainment of aṇimā and the rest as fruit; thereby having transcended the *mṛtyu* in the form of want of lordship, of adharma, desire, and the rest of the cluster of faults — *asambhūtyā*, by the upāsanā of avyākṛta, *amṛtam*, immortality of the form of *prakṛti-laya*, *aśnute*, attains.

Here in *sambhūtiṁ ca vināśaṁ ca* the indication is to be understood as proceeding by the elision of an *a*-letter (so that *vināśam* stands for *avināśam* — that is, *asambhūtim*), in conformity with the śruti that declares prakṛti-laya as the fruit.
IS_C01_V15: By a vessel of gold, the face of the True is hidden. That, O Pūṣan, do thou uncover, for the seeing by one whose dharma is the true.
IS_C01_V15::block-0:
The fruit attainable through human and divine wealth, defined by the śāstra and ending in *prakṛti-laya* — that is the entire range of saṁsāra-gati. Beyond this is what was declared earlier — *ātmaivābhūd vijānataḥ*: the becoming-everything, sarvātma-bhāva, which is the fruit of jñāna-niṣṭhā preceded by renunciation of all longings.

Thus the twofold sense of the Veda — characterized by pravṛtti and nivṛtti — has here been made manifest. For the unfolding of the entire pravṛtti-sense of the Veda, characterized by injunction and prohibition, the Brāhmaṇa portion ending with the Pravargya is employed; for the unfolding of the nivṛtti-sense, beyond this, the Bṛhadāraṇyaka is employed.

Now, he who, performing the rites from impregnation to cremation, wishes to live, together with the vidyā that has the lower Brahman as its object — for him it has been said, *vidyāṁ cāvidyāṁ ca yas tad vedobhayaṁ saha. avidyayā mṛtyuṁ tīrtvā vidyayāmṛtam aśnute* (Īśā Up. 11). By what path that adhikārin attains immortality is now stated.

*Tad yat tat satyam asau sa ādityo ya eṣa etasmin maṇḍale puruṣo yaścāyaṁ dakṣiṇe'kṣan puruṣaḥ* (Bṛ. Up. 5.5.2) — both these are Satya-Brahman; he who has worshipped it as Brahman, and who has performed the prescribed rites, on the approach of his end prays of the Satya-Self for the door to his own attainment —
IS_C01_V15::block-1: *Hiraṇmayena pātreṇa* — "hiraṇmaya" means as if golden, that is, full of light, luminous; by that as it were vessel — serving as a covering — *satyasya*, of Brahman situated in the sun's orb, *apihitam*, covered, *mukham*, the door — that, O *Pūṣan*, do thou *apāvṛṇu* — remove, draw aside — *satyadharmāya*: by my upāsanā of Thee as Satya, satya is my dharma — I am he whose dharma is the true; for me; or alternatively, for the performer of dharma as it truly is — *dṛṣṭaye* — for the seeing, the realization, of Thy true Self.
IS_C01_V16: O Pūṣan, sole seer, controller (Yama), Sūrya, son of Prajāpati, disperse your rays and gather up your blazing splendour. That most auspicious form of yours, that I behold. That Person who dwells yonder in the sun — He am I.
IS_C01_V16::block-0:
O Pūṣan — because he nourishes (poṣaṇa) the world, the sun is Pūṣan. So too, since he alone (eka) moves (ṛṣati, gacchati), he is Ekarṣi: O Ekarṣi. Likewise, because he restrains (saṃyamana) all, he is Yama: O Yama. And because he draws in (svīkaraṇa) the rays, the vital airs and the essences, he is Sūrya: O Sūrya. As son (apatya) of Prajāpati he is Prājāpatya: O Prājāpatya. Disperse (vyūha, vigamaya) your own rays. Gather up (samūha), draw together and withdraw your blazing light (tejas), your radiance. That form of yours which is most auspicious (kalyāṇatama), supremely beautiful — that I behold by your own grace.

Further, I do not beg of you as a servant: that Person (puruṣa) who stands within the orb of the sun, that one who is the embodiment of the vyāhṛtis — he is puruṣa because he has the form of a man (puruṣākāra), or because by him as prāṇa and intellect (buddhi) the whole world is filled (pūrṇa), hence puruṣa; or because he lies (śayana) in the city (purī) of the body, hence puruṣa. That very one am I.
IS_C01_V17: Let the vital breath now reach the immortal, all-pervading Air (the cosmic Sūtra-Ātman); and let this body end in ashes. Om! O mind (kratu), remember; remember what has been done. O kratu, remember; remember what has been done.
IS_C01_V17::block-0:
Now (atha), at this hour when I am about to die, let my vital air (vāyu, prāṇa), abandoning its limitation to the individual body (adhyātma-pariccheda), attain the all-pervading divine principle (adhidaivata-ātman), the immortal Air, the cosmic Sūtra-Ātman — this is the supplied sense of the verse. And it is to be understood that this subtle body (liṅga), refined by knowledge and works, is what departs, since otherwise the prayer for the path (in the next verse) would have no point. Then let this body, offered into fire, end in ashes (bhasmānta), with only ashes remaining.

The word 'Om' is taken according to the meditation prescribed: since Om is itself a symbol (pratīka) of Brahman, it here designates Brahman known as Fire (Agni), embodying truth, addressed in non-difference. O kratu — O power of resolve (saṅkalpātmaka) — remember (smara): the time has come for what is to be remembered by me; therefore remember whatever has been contemplated (bhāvita) over all this time. O Agni, remember the action (kṛta) which I have performed from childhood onwards — remember that too. The repetition 'kratu, remember; what has been done, remember' is for the sake of emphasis (ādara).
IS_C01_V18: O Agni, lead us by the good path to enjoyment of the fruits of works, O Deva who knowest all our deeds. Sever from us the crooked, deceitful sin. We shall offer thee abundant words of obeisance.
IS_C01_V18::block-0: Once again, by another mantra, he prays for the path —
IS_C01_V18::block-1:
O Agni, lead (naya, gamaya) by the good path (supatha), the auspicious road. The qualifier 'good' is meant to exclude the southern path. 'I am wearied,' he says, 'of the southern path which is marked by going and returning; therefore I beg of thee again and again — lead me by the auspicious path that is free of going and coming.' Rāye — for wealth, that is, for the enjoyment of the fruits of works. 'Lead us' — us who are endowed with the fruits of the dharma described — O Deva, who knowest all (viśvāni) our works (vayunāni), or our forms of insight.

Further, yuyodhi — separate, destroy — from us the crooked (juhurāṇa), the bent, the sin (enas) which is of the nature of deceit. The intention is: thus, becoming pure, we shall obtain the desired end. 'But we are now unable to render thee service' — therefore bhūyiṣṭhām, in greatest abundance, te, unto thee, namauktim, words of obeisance, vidhema, may we offer; that is, may we serve thee through homage.
IS_C01_OUTRO2::block-0:
Hearing the Śruti texts, 'Crossing death by avidyā, one attains immortality by vidyā' (Īśā 11) and 'Crossing death by destruction (vināśa), one attains immortality by non-becoming (asambhūti)' (Īśā 14), some entertain a doubt. To settle it we shall undertake a brief examination. First, what is the ground of the doubt? It is replied: Why is not the principal knowledge of the supreme Self (paramātma-vidyā) taken as the meaning of the word 'vidyā', and the immortality there spoken of as the absolute one?

'But,' it may be objected, 'between the knowledge of the supreme Self thus spoken of and works (karma) there is contradiction (virodha); hence their conjunction (samuccaya) is impossible.' True. Yet the contradiction is not perceived, because contradiction and non-contradiction alike are matters of scriptural authority. Just as the practice of avidyā (works) and the upāsanā of vidyā are alike enjoined by Śāstra, so too whether the two are mutually opposed or not is decided by Śāstra. As in the case where the rule 'Let none harm any being' which is known from Śāstra is again over-ridden by the very same Śāstra in 'In the sacrifice he should slay the animal,' so too may it be with vidyā and avidyā; and there may thus be conjunction of vidyā and karma.

No: for the Śruti says, 'Far apart and divergent are these two — that which is known as avidyā and that which is known as vidyā' (Kaṭha 1.2.4). If it be urged that, owing to the very text 'Both vidyā and avidyā,' there is no contradiction — no; for there is opposition between them in cause, in nature, and in fruit. If it be urged that, since alternation between contradiction and non-contradiction of vidyā and avidyā is not possible, the very fact that conjunction is enjoined proves there is no contradiction — no; because their simultaneous co-existence is unintelligible.

If it be said that vidyā and avidyā may be present successively in one and the same locus — no; for at the rise of vidyā avidyā has no being, and so avidyā cannot abide in that very locus. When the cognition arises that 'fire is hot and luminous,' there cannot, in the same locus where this cognition has arisen, also arise the avidyā that 'fire is cold or non-luminous.' Nor again can there arise mere doubt or non-cognition, since the Śruti, 'When to the knower all beings have become the very Self, what delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who beholds Oneness?' (Īśā 7), declares the impossibility of sorrow, delusion and the like.

We have already shown that, since avidyā cannot subsist, works which presuppose avidyā are likewise impossible. Therefore the 'immortality' obtained (in v. 11) is relative immortality. If the word 'vidyā' were taken in the sense of paramātma-vidyā, the prayer for the way out (through the door, etc.) in 'By a golden vessel...' (Īśā 15) would be inappropriate. Hence the conjunction is with upāsanā, not with the immediate knowledge of the supreme Self. So the meaning of the mantras stands as already explained, and here we conclude.
